newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn brinkmanship shows fault lines in Kohl team.
newsitem.headline: Bonn brinkmanship shows fault lines in Kohl team.

text.p: The bitter brinkmanship played out this week in Bonn has highlighted the balancing act Chancellor Helmut Kohl has to play to hold his coalition together while making Germany ready for Europe's single currency.

Kohl, who last week became Germany's longest-serving chancellor this century, almost lost his majority on Tuesday when his Free Democrat (FDP) partners rebelled against Finance Minister Theo Waigel's tax and budget policies.

This second show-down in a month made the 14-year coalition look like a marriage about to collapse. Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) seem unsure how to fix it and the FDP is set on scoring points off its bigger partner.

But like couples staying together "for the children", they are determined to stick it out rather than risk defeat in the 1998 election or the failure of their European dream. Also, the alternatives are less inviting than the rocky status quo.

"The continuation of the coalition was at stake," FDP parliamentary leader Hermann Otto Solms said of the tense meetings this week meant to find several billion marks to plug holes in the 1997 budget. "Anything was possible."

Juergen Moellemann, the party's biggest gambler, said he would lead FDP deputies from his North Rhine-Westphalia state in voting down the budget in parliament if Kohl and Waigel did not agree to cut a tax surcharge by two percentage points in 1998.

"The leaders of the coalition have lost all respect for each other," the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung commented. "Everyone has dug in so much and behaved so badly that the only way out could be a break-up that nobody really wants."
The business daily Handelsblatt agreed, saying: "The coalition is in a deep crisis."
The government seems hemmed in on all sides. With only a razor-thin 10-seat majority in parliament, it cannot risk making radical spending cuts that would make trade unions and vested interests howl.
The shaky FDP, which has gambled its political survival on its image as a tax-cutting party, refuses to let Waigel increase taxes to fill the budget gaps.

As the leading champion of Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU), Kohl cannot let new public borrowing break through the ceiling of three percent of GDP set by the Maastricht Treaty as a key qualification for the single currency.

Coalition sources said Kohl, eager to keep the FDP alive and at his side for the 1998 election, has given in to FDP pressure and agreed to the planned roll-back for the hated "solidarity tax", a surcharge to rebuild eastern Germany.
But, in a move to save face after so much tension, the actual decision to do this will only be announced next month with a package of other tax measures, the sources said.
That was only one part of the increasingly difficult search to keep the Maastricht cap on new borrowing.

Ministers face tough new battles over cuts in their 1997 budgets. Social spending could again be reduced and Defence Minister Volker Ruehe will have to fight hard to keep funds for the Eurofighter and other multinational arms projects.
One consideration keeping the coalition going is the fact that all partners think the alternatives are only worse.

Unlike in 1982, when it dumped Social Democrat (SPD) Chancellor Helmut Schmidt and formed the coalition with Kohl, the FDP does not have enough deputies in parliament to cross the aisle and form a centre-left coalition again.

The FDP, once a party of free speech and free markets, has demolished its old liberal wing so thoroughly in its years with Kohl that its sleek pro-business profile would not fit into a coalition with the SPD anyway.
The CDU theoretically has the option of a grand coalition with the SPD, but this is something its conservative Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union (CSU), abhors.
Switching to a grand coalition, a move Bonn pundits call an "elephants' wedding", would also rob the CDU of the biggest heavyweight it has.

"Kohl, who has fallen in love with his image as the chancellor who waits for his opportunities and then pounces, would hardly put up with being only half a chancellor in a grand coalition," the Frankfurter Allgemeine wrote.
